content: Magnolia grandiflora, commonly referred to as the Southern magnolia or bull bay, is a species of magnolia native to the southeastern United States. Its natural range extends from coastal North Carolina southward to central Florida and westward to East Texas. This tree is medium to large in size, typically reaching heights of 20 to 30 meters, and is notable for its striking appearance, both in its foliage and flowers. The leaves of the Southern magnolia are evergreen, simple, and broadly ovate in shape. They measure between 12 to 20 cm in length and 6 to 12 cm in width, with smooth margins. The upper surface of the leaves is dark green, stiff, and leathery, while the underside is often covered with yellow-brown pubescence, giving it a scurfy texture. In regions with severe winters, particularly at the northern limits of its cultivation, the leaves may bronze, blotch, or burn. However, most leaves remain attached to the tree until they are replaced by new foliage in the spring. In climates where the ground freezes, damage to the leaves is often caused more by winter sun exposure than by the cold itself. In the northern hemisphere, the south-facing side of the tree tends to experience more leaf damage compared to the north-facing side. There are two distinct leaf types: those with white undersides and those with brown undersides. The brown-leafed varieties are believed to be more cold-hardy than the white-leafed ones, though this has not been definitively proven. The flowers of the Southern magnolia are large, showy, and fragrant, with a citronella-like scent. They are white in color, can reach up to 30 cm in diameter, and consist of 6 to 12 waxy-textured petals. These flowers emerge from the tips of twigs on mature trees during late spring. Southern magnolia is a highly popular ornamental tree in the southeastern United States, valued for its attractive foliage and flowers. Along the East Coast, cold-hardy cultivars have been successfully planted as far north as the Ohio River. However, as one moves further north, large specimens become increasingly rare, eventually appearing only as shrubs before disappearing entirely from the landscape. For instance, mature trees are common in the Cincinnati, Ohio area but become smaller and less frequent further north, with few to no specimens found in Columbus, Ohio. In some gardens, this subtropical indicator tree can be seen as far north as Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, though cultivation becomes extremely challenging beyond this point. Near the northern limits of its range, the tree may suffer dieback from severe freezes but generally withstands normal freezing conditions well. On the West Coast, Southern magnolia is commonly found as far north as Vancouver, British Columbia. With the development of newer, more cold-hardy cultivars, the tree's cultivated range has expanded further north, with some specimens even being planted in the Chicago area. Notable cold-hardy varieties include 'Bracken's Brown Beauty,' 'Edith Bogue,' and '24 Below.' A dwarf cultivar known as Magnolia 'Little Gem' is also available in Australian nurseries. Southern magnolia holds the distinction of being the state tree of Mississippi.
